fetched_contents.text: O-arm CT for Confirmation of Successful Navigation During Robotic Assisted Bronchoscopy Background: Robotic assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) is designed to increase bronchoscopic accessibility for difficult to reach pulmonary lesions. One limitation to success of RAB is computed tomography (CT) to body divergence. Real time imaging with cone beam CT is increasingly utilized for confirmation of correct navigation and tool-in-lesion during RAB. O-arm CT is a 3-dimensional imaging modality, which has not previously been described for use with RAB. Our purpose is to display the feasibility, ease of use, and high rate of confirmation of tool-in-lesion when using O-arm CT during RAB. Methods: Single center, retrospective review of 75 patients undergoing RAB with intraprocedural use of O-arm CT. Results: Median patient age was 65 years. Forty-nine percent of cases involved nodules ≤2 cm. Bronchus sign was absent in 44% of cases. Median procedure time was 80 minutes. Median number of O-arm CT runs per case was 2. The median effective dose of radiation was 7.2 millisieverts. Tool-in-lesion was confirmed in 97% (77 of 79) of cases. Definitive diagnosis was reached in 61 to 68 of 79 cases (77% to 86%). There were 2 cases of pneumothorax (2.5%), one of which needed intervention with tube thoracostomy. Conclusions: O-arm CT is an effective, and convenient alternative to other 3-dimensional imaging modalities for intraprocedural confirmation of tool-in-lesion during RAB. Key Words: robotic assisted bronchoscopy, navigational bronchoscopy, O-arm ---------------------------------------- The adoption of low dose computed tomography (CT) for lung cancer screening has led to the identification of earlier stage lung cancers.1 In concert with increased health care utilization of chest imaging,2 a greater number of pulmonary nodules are now being identified. For nodules with intermediate to high risk for malignancy, expert consensus suggests the use of minimally invasive techniques such as, bronchoscopic biopsy or transthoracic needle biopsy (TTNB).3 TTNB is limited by its relatively high rate of pneumothorax.4 Electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy (ENB) has been used to navigate to peripheral lung lesions and perform biopsies with lower rates of pneumothorax.5–7 However, with this technology, diagnostic yield continues to be inferior to TTNB.8,9 Potential limitations include the articulation and reach of the handheld video bronchoscopes used during ENB, as well as the inability of navigation probes to maintain a static position when tools are introduced and retracted from the working channel. Recently, robotic assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) (RAB is meant to be inclusive of shape sensing robotic assisted bronchoscopy AND electromagnetic robotic assisted bronchoscopy) has been developed to overcome some challenges encountered when using ENB. Shape sensing robotic bronchoscopes have the ability to articulate 180 degrees in 4 directions and have a longer length than traditional handheld bronchoscopes. This greater articulation along with more precise movements allow access into previously arduous airways.10 Despite these advances, high diagnostic yield during RAB continues to be elusive.11,12 CT to body divergence is thought to be a significant deterrent for successful navigation to target lesions in ENB and RAB.13 A myriad of factors contributes to CT to body divergence. Variations in lung volumes before versus during the procedure may be one of the most notable contributors. Lung volumes on the preprocedure chest CT obtained at full inspiration, vary drastically from intraprocedural mechanical ventilation providing volumes close to tidal breathing. Nodules have been demonstrated to vary in position by nearly 2 cm with these large differences in lung volumes.14 In some cases, the variation may be greater than the size of the lesion itself, leaving little margin for error and contributing to nondiagnostic biopsies. To overcome this divergence, many centers now supplement RAB or ENB with 3-dimentional (3D) imaging obtained during the procedure. One common modality is cone beam CT (CBCT) with augmented fluoroscopy. Studies with both ENB and RAB have demonstrated higher diagnostic yield when using CBCT for confirmation of tool-in-lesion.15,16 CBCT, however, can be expensive and may not be readily available at all institutions for use during pulmonary procedures. O-arm CT is an alternative imaging modality which may be more accessible and affordable for pulmonary procedures at some centers. The O-arm CT is a mobile machine which functions much like a conventional, stationary CT scanner found in most hospitals. The O-arm CT has a gantry which can be opened into the shape of a “C”. This gantry shape is used when the machine is being transported or positioned around a patient. Once in position, the gantry is closed to encircle the patient, forming the “O” shape. Further adjustments can be made by moving the whole unit toward the head or foot of the bed. Rotating x-rays performed around the gantry then allow for reconstruction of images in the axial, sagittal, and coronal planes Traditionally, O-arm CT has been used in spinal, cranial, or orthopedic procedures, and is rarely seen in literature related to pulmonary nodules. However, it has been described as a useful tool for intraoperative location of nonpalpable nodules during video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery.17 In addition, O-arm CT has recently been described as a technically feasible option for use during ENB.18 The use of O-arm CT during RAB has not previously been described. Here we present a retrospective review of our experience using O-arm CT during RAB for secondary confirmation of successful navigation to lung lesions. fetched_contents.text: Diagnostic yield and safety of navigation bronchoscopy: A systematic review and meta-analysis 1. Introduction Peripheral pulmonary nodules are a common finding and often present a diagnostic challenge. The increased resolution of CT, the increased use of CT for a variety of indications (for both pulmonary and non-pulmonary disease), and the implementation of CT screening programs have led to an increase in their incidence [1]. When these pulmonary nodules are suspected to be malignant, as determined by prediction models utilizing patient and nodule characteristics, image-guided minimally invasive biopsy is indicated [2]. Navigation bronchoscopy is a frequently performed method to sample peripheral pulmonary nodules. Conventionally, it conveyed fluoroscopy-guided transbronchial biopsy by a standard flexible bronchoscope, with a limited diagnostic yield of around 37% [3]. To improve diagnostic yield, new technologies were developed. Electromagnetic navigation (EMN) and virtual bronchoscopy (VB) were primarily aimed at optimizing navigation. Ultrathin bronchoscopy (UTB) was often utilized in combination with VB and facilitated the navigation process but also offered direct visualization. Radial endobronchial ultrasound (rEBUS) did not offer any additional navigation possibilities but could confirm correct positioning. In a meta-analysis, Wang-Memoli et al. already showed in 2012 that these techniques were able to obtain a navigation success of 95% and a diagnostic yield of 70% [4], illustrating that with navigation assistance considerable improvements in diagnostic yield could be achieved, but there was still a discrepancy between reaching the target and obtaining a diagnosis. Newer technologies integrating advanced imaging support have aimed to reduce this gap. Pre-existing techniques such as cone-beam CT are now being applied for navigation bronchoscopy (CBCT-NB) and can be used as a navigation technique but also gives precise positioning confirmation [5]. The implementation of tomosynthesis techniques in EMN aims at reducing CT to body divergence resulting in more accurate sampling (fEMN) [6]. Robot-assisted bronchoscopy (RB), aims at further optimizing navigation accuracy, positioning, and tissue sampling [7]. The combined use of these techniques might further increase diagnostic yield [5]. There is a growing body of literature on these different techniques, with unfortunately a large amount of heterogeneity in the definitions used for outcomes such as diagnostic yield. This makes it difficult to compare results across studies, especially because it is not always clearly reported which definition researchers applied. A recent study has increased interest in creating more uniform definitions to improve the comparability of different studies [8]. Given the development of new technologies and their increased combined use in the last decade, it is important to assess if diagnostic yield for pulmonary nodule evaluation has improved while applying the newly proposed definitions for reporting this outcome. This systematic review evaluates the diagnostic yield and safety of navigation bronchoscopy in the diagnostic work-up of patients with peripheral pulmonary nodules suspected of lung cancer. 2. Methods 2.1. Search strategy and study selection Using the search strategies in supplemental Table S1, we searched Embase, Medline, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) for primary diagnostic studies published from inception to the 6th of May 2022. Subsequently, two researchers independently assessed titles and abstracts of all retrieved records for potential relevance and disagreements were discussed. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were independently assessed for final inclusion by both researchers. Again, discrepancies were discussed until a consensus was reached. Additionally, previously published systematic reviews were checked for missed studies, which were included for further assessment if found (n = 14) [9], [10], [11]. We included primary studies that evaluated the diagnostic accuracy or diagnostic yield of EMN, VB, CBCT, or RB as the primary navigation tool in patients with peripheral pulmonary nodules suspected of lung cancer. We excluded studies focusing on other navigation techniques as the sole tool under investigation, such as (augmented) fluoroscopy (AF), UTB,and rEBUS. These tools assist in the navigation process but are not a strict navigation technique itself. However, we included studies performed in a multi-modality setting, where a combination of navigation techniques (e.g., CBCT with EMN or VB with UTB) was used. We excluded studies with average or median pulmonary nodule sizes larger than 3 cm (limiting lesion size to T1 tumors[12]), or studies explicitly reporting that lesions could be reached with traditional bronchoscopy. We also excluded studies with tumor marking as research aim (e.g. marking of a nodule with a radiopaque marker with the aim to assist in surgery), studies in languages other than English, or studies including <10 study participants. 2.2. Data extraction For every included study, one researcher extracted the following data, which was checked by a second researcher: type of data collection (prospective versus retrospective), number of patients and lesions included, size of pulmonary nodules, navigation technique, additional navigation tools used, sampling tools used, if a structured sampling strategy was described, bronchus sign, nodule location, diagnostic yield, and adverse events. If a study compared two different navigation techniques (e.g. VB vs EMN), data from the subgroups were extracted separately. If a study compared aspects of a procedure (e.g. VB with guide sheath vs. VB with UTB) data were extracted separately. In cases where a study had more than one study arm, but only one of those arms fulfilled the inclusion criteria, only this study arm was included. 2.3. fetched_contents.text: Advanced Imaging for Robotic Bronchoscopy: A Review Abstract Recent advances in navigational platforms have led bronchoscopists to make major strides in diagnostic interventions for pulmonary parenchymal lesions. Over the last decade, multiple platforms including electromagnetic navigation and robotic bronchoscopy have allowed bronchoscopists to safely navigate farther into the lung parenchyma with increased stability and accuracy. Limitations persist, even with these newer technologies, in achieving a similar or higher diagnostic yield when compared to the transthoracic computed tomography (CT) guided needle approach. One of the major limitations to this effect is due to CT-to-body divergence. Real-time feedback that better defines the tool–lesion relationship is vital and can be obtained with additional imaging using radial endobronchial ultrasound, C-arm based tomosynthesis, cone-beam CT (fixed or mobile), and O-arm CT. Herein, we describe the role of this adjunct imaging with robotic bronchoscopy for diagnostic purposes, describe potential strategies to counteract the CT-to-body divergence phenomenon, and address the potential role of advanced imaging for lung tumor ablation. Keywords: robotic bronchoscopy, cone-beam CT, C-arm based tomosynthesis, CIOS spin, O-arm CT, ventilator strategies, navigational bronchoscopy, CT-to-body divergence 1. Introduction Lung nodules are discovered on chest computed tomography (CT) images over 25% of the time, and in approximately 1.6 million people annually in the US [1]. Incidental and screening-detected nodules are expected to rise with the increased use of chest CT for the diagnosis of advanced lung diseases including emphysema, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, as well as the liberalized guidelines for lung cancer screening [2]. Approximately 95% of all nodules detected on imaging are benign, but in high-risk populations (i.e., age 50–80 years, >20 pack year smoking, smoking within the last 15 years, personal history of cancer, family history of lung cancer) a timely and minimally invasive diagnostic modality would expedite the management of a potentially malignant nodule while minimizing testing for patients with a benign nodule. The approach utilizing bronchoscopy as a diagnostic method is the preferred technique for evaluating lung nodules suspicious for lung cancer due to the safety profile and because it allows for concurrent staging via endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of the mediastinal, hilar, and interlobar lymph nodes [3]. Recent advances in robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) have enabled chest physicians to safely navigate within the lung and sample parenchymal pulmonary lesions (PPL) with more confidence and increasing accuracy. Advantages of these navigation platforms are enhanced maneuverability, farther reach, and increased stability of the bronchoscope as compared to conventional guided bronchoscopy, but their diagnostic yield remains to be improved [4,5,6,7,8]. These platforms guide the bronchoscopist by creating a virtual pathway to a target lesion, but limitations in the accuracy remain due to the absence of real-time guidance. Additional technologies such as radial EBUS (rEBUS), augmented fluoroscopy with C-arm based tomography (CABT), or cone-beam CT (CBCT) may be used for real-time confirmation of lesion location and confirmation of “tool in lesion” prior to sampling. CT-to-Body Divergence Regardless of the navigation platform used, a planning CT is created with a thin-cut chest CT scan which is obtained with the patient at the end of an inspiratory hold maneuver with lung volume close to total lung capacity (TLC). This maneuver helps enhance the airway detection (segmentation) on the planning software and offers a better navigation path selection. The target PPL is identified on the virtual airway tree and its relationship to the airway is defined. During the procedure, the virtual reconstruction of the airway and the relative location of the target PPL is synchronized with the position of the robotic bronchoscope and the patient’s anatomy in vivo via a process called registration (Figure 1). Once registration is complete, the operator navigates to the target lesion by using the virtually mapped pathway. However, the lung volume of the CT scan used for procedural planning (at full inspiration, breath hold, and nearing total lung capacity) is different than the patient’s lung volume at the time of the procedure (mechanical breathing under general anesthesia and paralysis with volume nearing functional residual capacity), potentially leading to a phenomenon known as CT-to-body divergence (CTBD). CTBD is the difference between PPL location at the time of planning CT and at the time of procedure. Other than the differences in lung volume, the development of atelectasis during the procedure related to ventilation strategies, oxygen supplementation, and manipulation of the airway with tools, can lead to further worsening of CTBD [9]. Hence, secondary to this phenomenon, the navigation system’s feedback could be misleading and provide a false reassurance of successful localization to a virtual target when in fact the scope may be off the real target (Figure 2). This is particularly true for nodules in the lower lobes due to more prevalent atelectasis during general anesthesia. CTBD has been evaluated in multiple studies. Chen and colleagues performed two chest CT scans for patients undergoing navigation bronchoscopy at full inspiration and at tidal volume breathing, which demonstrated a mean deviation of 17 mm of nodules between two scans [10]. A study using the IonTM RAB platform identified that CTBD was present in 50% of the nodules, with divergence defined as an overlap of less than 10% between the target location on the preoperative CT and the target location during real-time mobile 3D imaging; this rate increased to 60% when CTBD was redefined based on 10 mm distance bet…

Technical and operational value of O-arm CT in bronchoscopy

O-arm CT provides real-time cross-sectional imaging and spatial orientation by offering 3-dimensional imaging during the procedure, which allows intraprocedural confirmation of tool-in-lesion and helps verify the exact location of the bronchoscope relative to the target lesion [N1-F1]. The system functions like a conventional CT scanner but is mobile and can be positioned around the patient, with a gantry that can be opened into a “C” shape and closed into an “O” shape for scanning [N1-F1]. This design supports axial, sagittal, and coronal plane reconstruction, which is important for spatial orientation during bronchoscopy [N1-F1]. In robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB), it is described as a convenient alternative to other 3-dimensional imaging modalities for confirming successful navigation and tool-in-lesion [N1-R1]. In practice, it is used to confirm whether the robotic bronchoscope has reached the target lesion, thereby improving the proceduralist’s ability to make a decision about sampling or biopsy [N1-F1].

The bronchoscopy tasks most enhanced by O-arm CT guidance are those requiring precise localization of the scope to the target lesion and confirmation of tool-in-lesion before tissue sampling. In the study cited, O-arm CT was used during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy to confirm successful navigation and to guide biopsy decisions, and tool-in-lesion was confirmed in 97% of cases [N1-F1]. It also appears to support bronchoscopic navigation workflows where real-time imaging is needed to reduce the risk of false localization and to improve confidence in the bronchoscopist’s decision-making [N2-R1]. The broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy suggests that CBCT-guided navigation bronchoscopy integrates navigation guidance, tool-in-lesion confirmation, and tissue acquisition, reinforcing the role of real-time imaging in workflow efficiency and accuracy [N2-R1]. In this context, O-arm CT fits as a real-time imaging adjunct that helps the proceduralist navigate difficult anatomy and confirm lesion contact.

The main trade-offs between speed, image quality, and radiation exposure are apparent from the evidence. O-arm CT provides high-quality, cross-sectional imaging that supports precise spatial orientation, but it is not instantaneous; it requires a scanning procedure that adds time to the bronchoscopy workflow [N1-F1]. The study reports a median number of O-arm CT runs per case of 2 and a median procedure time of 80 minutes, indicating that the system can be used repeatedly but does not eliminate procedural time [N1-F1]. On the radiation side, the evidence states that O-arm CT has a median effective dose of 7.2 millisieverts, with a wide interquartile range from 3.9 to 14.3 mSv, suggesting that radiation exposure is a meaningful constraint [N5-R1]. The same source also notes that CBCT navigation bronchoscopy has been described as having low radiation exposure for patient and staff and as a cost-effective strategy, which implies that radiation burden is a key practical limitation compared with other imaging-guided approaches [N5-R3]. Taken together, O-arm CT improves spatial accuracy and confidence, but its value must be balanced against procedural time and radiation exposure [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

Clinical evidence on diagnostic yield and procedural outcomes

The evidence indicates that O-arm CT improves detection of clinically relevant lesions by helping confirm tool-in-lesion and by reducing the risk of false navigation. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, tool-in-lesion was confirmed in 97% of cases, and definitive diagnosis was reached in 61 to 68 of 79 cases (77% to 86%) [N1-F1]. This suggests that the system helps identify cases in which the bronchoscope is actually in contact with the target lesion, thereby improving the likelihood of obtaining a meaningful diagnostic sample. The study also reports that the adoption of low-dose CT for lung cancer screening has led to more pulmonary nodules being identified, and that expert consensus suggests using minimally invasive techniques such as bronchoscopic biopsy for intermediate- to high-risk nodules [N1-F1]. The implication is that O-arm CT supports more precise sampling of those nodules, especially those that are small or difficult to reach.

In terms of how diagnostic yield compares with standard bronchoscopy, the broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy provides important context. A systematic review and meta-analysis states that conventional navigation bronchoscopy had a diagnostic yield of around 37% before the development of advanced techniques, and that navigation techniques improved diagnostic yield to 70% [N3-F2]. Another source reports that diagnostic yield after follow-up was 72.1% for nodules <20 mm and 69.7% for ≥20 mm, which suggests that yield varies by lesion size [N3-R2]. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, the reported diagnostic yield was 77% to 86% when definitive diagnosis was defined as a specific malignant or benign process [N1-F1]. This is notably higher than the standard navigational bronchoscopy yield of around 70% [N3-F2], but the exact comparison depends on the definition of diagnostic yield and the population studied [N3-F2]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that O-arm CT-guided RAB improves yield, but it does not yet establish a universally standardized benchmark across all bronchoscopy settings.

The yield improvements appear partially sustained across lesion types and anatomy, but the evidence is mixed and context-dependent. The study explicitly notes that 49% of cases involved nodules ≤2 cm, and that bronchus sign was absent in 44% of cases [N1-F1]. This indicates that O-arm CT may be particularly useful in small or difficult-to-reach nodules. The broader literature also shows that electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB) has been used for peripheral lung lesions and that robotic-assisted bronchoscopy aims to further optimize navigation accuracy [N4-F3]. In a comparison of CBCT-guided robotic navigation with electromagnetic navigation, one trial reported that ssRAB-CBCT had a higher diagnostic yield than ENB-CBCT, with 70.1% versus 66%, respectively [N7-R2]. This suggests that yield gains may be better sustained in robotic systems when combined with advanced imaging, but the benefit may vary by lesion type and anatomy. The evidence also notes that diagnostic yield is limited by CT-to-body divergence and that real-time imaging helps counteract this phenomenon [N4-F3], implying that yield improvements are strongest when the system can compensate for anatomical changes during the procedure.

Overall, the clinical evidence suggests that O-arm CT improves detection of clinically relevant lesions and increases diagnostic yield compared with conventional navigational bronchoscopy, especially for small and difficult-to-reach nodules. However, the evidence base is still evolving, and yield improvements are partially sustained across lesion types and anatomy, with some studies showing modest gains and others showing more substantial differences depending on the system used [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3][N7-R2].
node_outputs.N10:
Limitations, risks, and practical barriers to adoption

The main complications and safety concerns associated with O-arm CT use include pneumothorax and radiation exposure. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, there were 2 cases of pneumothorax, one of which required intervention with tube thoracostomy [N1-F1]. This is an important safety concern because bronchoscopy itself can carry the risk of pneumothorax, and O-arm CT use adds another potential complication. The same study also reports a median effective dose of 7.2 mSv, with a wide range from 3.9 to 14.3 mSv, indicating that radiation exposure is a meaningful limitation [N5-R1]. The broader literature on CBCT navigation bronchoscopy notes that guided bronchoscopy has a favorable safety profile, but radiation exposure remains a concern when compared with percutaneous image-guided lung biopsy [N5-R2]. Another source explicitly states that CBCT navigation bronchoscopy has been described as having low radiation exposure for patient and staff and as a cost-effective strategy, but this does not eliminate the exposure entirely [N5-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a risk profile that is acceptable for many cases, but not negligible, and that radiation exposure is a key limitation to consider.

Cost, availability, and workflow constraints are also important barriers. O-arm CT is described as a mobile machine that may be more accessible and affordable at some centers compared with fixed CBCT systems [N1-F1]. However, the study also notes that CBCT is expensive and may not be readily available at all institutions [N1-F1]. The same source describes O-arm CT as a technically feasible option for use during ENB, but it is not widely established in pulmonary nodule literature [N1-F1]. In addition, the workflow implications of O-arm CT are clear from the reported median procedure time of 80 minutes and median number of O-arm CT runs per case of 2 [N1-F1]. These data suggest that the system adds procedural time and may disrupt the flow of the bronchoscopy session, especially if multiple scans are needed per case. The evidence also points to the need for reduced-range CT scanning protocols to minimize radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic utility [N5-R4], which implies that workflow optimization is necessary for adoption.

The patient and procedural scenarios least suitable for O-arm CT are those where rapid imaging is critical, radiation exposure is especially sensitive, or the proceduralist cannot tolerate added time. The evidence suggests that the system is most useful when precise localization and tool-in-lesion confirmation are needed, such as in small or difficult-to-reach nodules [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Conversely, it is less suitable when the patient’s anatomy is highly unstable, when rapid decision-making is required, or when the institution lacks the infrastructure to support mobile CT scanning [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy also indicates that yield improvements depend on accurate registration and real-time imaging, which may be more challenging in difficult anatomical settings [N4-F3]. Therefore, O-arm CT is a powerful tool where it is feasible to integrate it into the bronchoscopy workflow, but it is not ideal for all clinical settings and should be used selectively.

Evidence comparing O-arm CT with other navigational bronchoscopy systems

O-arm CT differs from electromagnetic navigation (ENB) and shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy (ssRAB) primarily in its imaging modality and role within the workflow. O-arm CT is a 3-dimensional imaging modality used for intraprocedural confirmation of tool-in-lesion and for providing cross-sectional spatial orientation during bronchoscopy [N1-F1][N1-R1]. In contrast, ENB and ssRAB are navigation platforms that guide the bronchoscope to the target lesion, while O-arm CT is an adjunct imaging system that confirms whether the scope has reached the lesion [N4-F3]. The literature explicitly states that robotic-assisted bronchoscopy includes both shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy and electromagnetic robotic bronchoscopy, and that O-arm CT is used as an alternative to other 3-dimensional imaging modalities during RAB [N1-F1]. This distinction is important: ENB and ssRAB provide navigation guidance, whereas O-arm CT provides real-time imaging confirmation of localization.

In terms of performance on diagnostic yield and procedural success, the evidence suggests that O-arm CT-guided robotic bronchoscopy can improve yield, but the exact superiority depends on the comparison system. A trial comparing CBCT-guided robotic navigation with electromagnetic navigation reported that ssRAB-CBCT had a higher diagnostic yield than ENB-CBCT, with 70.1% versus 66%, respectively [N7-R2]. Another source states that robotic shape-sensing navigation bronchoscopy combined with advanced C-arm 3D imaging yielded a high diagnostic accuracy with minimal complications [N7-R5]. This implies that O-arm CT is not necessarily the only superior system, but it can be part of a more accurate workflow. The broader review also notes that navigation techniques using advanced imaging and robotics are more promising than conventional methods, with robotic bronchoscopy aiming to improve accuracy and stability [N4-F3]. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, O-arm CT was used to confirm tool-in-lesion and to support biopsy decisions, with a very high rate of tool-in-lesion confirmation (97%) and a substantial diagnostic yield [N1-F1].

The study designs and outcome measures supporting these comparisons are mixed but informative. The robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study is a retrospective review of 79 cases [N1-F1]. The ssRAB vs ENB comparison is a trial-based study with defined diagnostic yield endpoints [N7-R2]. The review on advanced imaging for robotic bronchoscopy uses a systematic review and meta-analysis approach, comparing outcomes across multiple navigation platforms and noting heterogeneity in definitions [N4-F3]. The broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy also includes prospective and retrospective studies, and the evidence emphasizes that outcome measures such as diagnostic yield are often not uniformly defined, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-F2]. Nevertheless, the available evidence supports the conclusion that O-arm CT can enhance yield when used as an adjunct imaging system, and that robotic platforms with advanced imaging tend to perform better than conventional navigation alone [N1-F1][N4-F3][N7-R2].

The same source also notes that CBCT navigation bronchoscopy has been described as having low radiation exposure for patient and staff and as a cost-effective strategy, which implies that radiation burden is a key practical limitation compared with other imaging-guided approaches [N5-R3]. Taken together, O-arm CT improves spatial accuracy and confidence, but its value must be balanced against procedural time and radiation exposure [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

## What impact does O-arm CT have on diagnostic yield?

The evidence indicates that O-arm CT improves the detection of **clinically relevant lesions** by helping confirm tool-in-lesion and by reducing the risk of false navigation [N1-F1]. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, the reported diagnostic yield was 77% to 86% when definitive diagnosis was defined as a specific malignant or benign process [N1-F1]. This is notably higher than the standard navigational bronchoscopy yield of around 37% before the development of advanced techniques, and later improved to around 70% with navigation assistance [N3-F2]. The broader literature also reports that diagnostic yield after follow-up was 72.1% for nodules <20 mm and 69.7% for ≥20 mm, which suggests that yield varies by lesion size [N3-R2].

In terms of comparison with standard bronchoscopy, the evidence supports a clear trend: advanced imaging-guided bronchoscopy improves yield substantially. A systematic review and meta-analysis states that conventional navigation bronchoscopy had a diagnostic yield of around 37% before the development of advanced techniques, and that navigation techniques improved diagnostic yield to 70% [N3-F2]. The robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study adds that O-arm CT-guided RAB can achieve even higher yield, with definitive diagnosis reached in 77% to 86% of cases [N1-F1]. This suggests that O-arm CT is not just an incremental improvement but can meaningfully raise yield, especially when the procedure is difficult or when the lesion is small or difficult to reach [N4-F3].

Yield improvements appear **partially sustained across lesion types and anatomy**, but the evidence is mixed and context-dependent. The study explicitly notes that 49% of cases involved nodules ≤2 cm, and that bronchus sign was absent in 44% of cases [N1-F1]. This indicates that O-arm CT may be particularly useful in small or difficult-to-reach nodules. The broader literature also shows that electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB) has been used for peripheral lung lesions and that robotic-assisted bronchoscopy aims to further optimize navigation accuracy [N4-F3]. In a comparison of CBCT-guided robotic navigation with electromagnetic navigation, one trial reported that ssRAB-CBCT had a higher diagnostic yield than ENB-CBCT, with 70.1% versus 66%, respectively [N7-R2]. This suggests that yield gains may be better sustained in robotic systems when combined with advanced imaging, but the benefit may vary by lesion type and anatomy. The evidence also notes that diagnostic yield is limited by CT-to-body divergence and that real-time imaging helps counteract this phenomenon [N4-F3], implying that yield improvements are strongest when the system can compensate for anatomical changes during the procedure.

## How does O-arm CT compare with other navigational bronchoscopy systems?

O-arm CT differs from **electromagnetic navigation (ENB)** and **shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy (ssRAB)** primarily in its imaging modality and role within the workflow. O-arm CT is a **3-dimensional imaging modality** used for intraprocedural confirmation of tool-in-lesion and for providing cross-sectional spatial orientation during bronchoscopy [N1-F1][N1-R1]. In contrast, ENB and ssRAB are navigation platforms that guide the bronchoscope to the target lesion, while O-arm CT is an **adjunct imaging system** that confirms whether the scope has reached the lesion [N4-F3]. The literature explicitly states that robotic-assisted bronchoscopy includes both shape-sensing robotic bronchoscopy and electromagnetic robotic bronchoscopy, and that O-arm CT is used as an alternative to other 3-dimensional imaging modalities during RAB [N1-F1]. This distinction is important: ENB and ssRAB provide navigation guidance, whereas O-arm CT provides real-time imaging confirmation of localization.

In terms of performance on diagnostic yield and procedural success, the evidence suggests that O-arm CT-guided robotic bronchoscopy can improve yield, but the exact superiority depends on the comparison system. A trial comparing CBCT-guided robotic navigation with electromagnetic navigation reported that ssRAB-CBCT had a higher diagnostic yield than ENB-CBCT, with 70.1% versus 66%, respectively [N7-R2]. Another source states that robotic shape-sensing navigation bronchoscopy combined with advanced C-arm 3D imaging yielded a high diagnostic accuracy with minimal complications [N7-R5]. This implies that O-arm CT is not necessarily the only superior system, but it can be part of a more accurate workflow. The broader review also notes that navigation techniques using advanced imaging and robotics are more promising than conventional methods, with robotic bronchoscopy aiming to improve accuracy and stability [N4-F3]. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, O-arm CT was used to confirm tool-in-lesion and to support biopsy decisions, with a very high rate of tool-in-lesion confirmation (97%) and a substantial diagnostic yield [N1-F1].

The study designs and outcome measures supporting these comparisons are mixed but informative. The robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study is a **retrospective review** of 79 cases [N1-F1]. The ssRAB vs ENB comparison is a **trial-based study** with defined diagnostic yield endpoints [N7-R2]. The review on advanced imaging for robotic bronchoscopy uses a **systematic review and meta-analysis** approach, comparing outcomes across multiple navigation platforms and noting heterogeneity in definitions [N4-F3]. The broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy also includes **prospective and retrospective studies**, and the evidence emphasizes that outcome measures such as diagnostic yield are often not uniformly defined, making direct comparisons difficult [N3-F2]. Nevertheless, the available evidence supports the conclusion that O-arm CT can enhance yield when used as an adjunct imaging system, and that robotic platforms with advanced imaging tend to perform better than conventional navigation alone [N1-F1][N4-F3][N7-R2].

## Limitations and practical barriers to adoption

The main complications and safety concerns associated with O-arm CT use include **pneumothorax** and **radiation exposure**. In the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study, there were 2 cases of pneumothorax, one of which required intervention with tube thoracostomy [N1-F1]. The same study also reports a median effective dose of 7.2 mSv, with a wide range from 3.9 to 14.3 mSv, indicating that radiation exposure is a meaningful limitation [N5-R1]. The broader literature on CBCT navigation bronchoscopy notes that guided bronchoscopy has a favorable safety profile, but radiation exposure remains a concern when compared with percutaneous image-guided lung biopsy [N5-R2]. Another source explicitly states that CBCT navigation bronchoscopy has been described as having low radiation exposure for patient and staff and as a cost-effective strategy, but this does not eliminate the exposure entirely [N5-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a risk profile that is acceptable for many cases, but not negligible, and that radiation exposure is a key limitation to consider.

Cost, availability, and workflow constraints are also important barriers. O-arm CT is described as a mobile machine that may be more accessible and affordable at some centers compared with fixed CBCT systems [N1-F1]. However, the study also notes that CBCT is expensive and may not be readily available at all institutions [N1-F1]. The same source describes O-arm CT as a technically feasible option for use during ENB, but it is not widely established in pulmonary nodule literature [N1-F1]. In addition, the workflow implications of O-arm CT are clear from the reported median procedure time of 80 minutes and median number of O-arm CT runs per case of 2 [N1-F1]. These data suggest that the system adds procedural time and may disrupt the flow of the bronchoscopy session, especially if multiple scans are needed per case. The evidence also points to the need for **reduced-range CT scanning protocols** to minimize radiation exposure while maintaining diagnostic utility [N5-R4], which implies that workflow optimization is necessary for adoption.

The patient and procedural scenarios least suitable for O-arm CT are those where **rapid imaging** is critical, **radiation exposure** is especially sensitive, or the proceduralist cannot tolerate **added time**. The evidence suggests that the system is most useful when precise localization and tool-in-lesion confirmation are needed, such as in small or difficult-to-reach nodules [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Conversely, it is less suitable when the patient’s anatomy is highly unstable, when rapid decision-making is required, or when the institution lacks the infrastructure to support mobile CT scanning [N5-R1][N5-R3]. The broader literature on navigational bronchoscopy also indicates that yield improvements depend on accurate registration and real-time imaging, which may be more challenging in difficult anatomical settings [N4-F3]. Therefore, O-arm CT is a powerful tool where it is feasible to integrate it into the bronchoscopy workflow, but it is not ideal for all clinical settings and should be used selectively.

## Bottom line

Overall, O-arm CT enhances real-time navigation by providing **3D cross-sectional imaging** and **tool-in-lesion confirmation** during bronchoscopy, which improves spatial orientation and confidence in localization [N1-F1][N1-R1]. It appears to improve **diagnostic yield**, particularly for small or difficult-to-reach lesions, with reported diagnostic yields around 77% to 86% in the robotic-assisted bronchoscopy study and higher gains compared with conventional navigational bronchoscopy [N1-F1][N3-F2]. However, its use comes with trade-offs: it adds **procedural time** and **radiation exposure**, and it is not a perfect solution for every case [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3]. Compared with other navigational systems, O-arm CT is best understood as an **adjunct imaging system** that supports robotic or electromagnetic navigation, rather than as a replacement for them [N4-F3]. The strongest evidence supports its value in settings where precise localization is difficult, but its adoption depends on the institution’s workflow, resource availability, and the patient’s clinical scenario [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].
